The creed of monotheism (*tawḥīd*) is that there is no doer, no benefiter, and no harmer except Allah Exalted, and that none is invoked alongside Him, as He Exalted said: ﴿So do not invoke anyone with Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. And the Prophet ﷺ, although he is the most exalted in rank with Allah Exalted of all mankind, the greatest of people in standing and love, and the nearest to Him, has no part in the affair, and does not possess for people any harm, benefit, guidance, or anything else, as is stated in the text of the Qur'an.

He is only a conveyor of the message from Allah Exalted, and one does not draw near to Allah Exalted except by acting upon what came through his tongue ﷺ, and following what the Companions, the Successors, and the rightly-guided imams who exercised independent judgment followed of his guidance and sunnah. There is no means for bringing benefits and warding off harms except what Allah has guided people to. There is no meaning to seeking intercession through a Prophet or a saint except by following him and emulating him. Many verses revealed in the Mighty Qur'an guide us to this, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31] ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153], and others besides these verses. If this is the correct position, I hope to have it confirmed in writing, so that I may defend myself against one who has thought ill of me.

He, may God have mercy on him, replied after the basmala and the hawqala: Your belief is this, and it is the correct belief, with no admixture of error, and it is what every Muslim who believes in what Muhammad ﷺ brought must hold; for the foundation upon which the mission of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ grows is this meaning of monotheism, as Allah said: ﴿Say, He is Allah, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1] ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2]. *Al-Samad* is the one who is turned to in needs, and to whom those who nurture (others) turn for help in what they seek, and for strength when their own powers fail. Expressing the predicate in this form conveys restriction (*ḥaṣr*), as is known among the people of the language; so there is no *samad* except Him.

He has guided us to the obligation of directing oneself to Him alone in the clearest expression, in His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186]. Shaykh Muhyi al-Din Ibn al-ʿArabi, the shaykh of the Sufis, said on page 226 of the fourth volume of his *al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya*, in discussing this verse: Indeed, Allah Exalted has not left a proof for His servant against Him. Rather, the conclusive proof belongs to Allah. So one does not seek nearness to Him through anything other than Him, for seeking nearness is only the pursuit of closeness to Him, and Allah has informed us that He is near, and His report is true. End of quote, summarized.

Moreover, those who claim the permissibility of some of what the common people do today in this matter only speak about it in vague terms, and they follow paths of interpretation that do not correspond to what is in people's hearts. They interpret *jāh* and *wāsiṭah* (intermediary) in ways that have no effect on the imaginations of those who hold the belief. What state would compel them to this? Before them are the first three generations, and there was none of this seeking of intercession in them, nor anything resembling it in any way. The books of the Sunnah and the biographies are before us as witnesses to this. Everything that came into being after that is, at the least of its descriptions, a *bidʿah* (innovation) in religion, and every innovation is misguidance, and every misguidance is in the Fire.

The worst of innovations is that in which there is a semblance of associating partners with Allah Exalted and of having ill opinion of Him, such as these innovations we are discussing. It seems to these claimants that this is an exaltation of the status of the Prophet ﷺ, or of the Prophets, or of the saints, although the best exaltation of the Prophets is to stop at what they brought, and to avoid adding to what they legislated by the permission of their Lord. The exaltation of the saints is by choosing what they chose for themselves. The thought of these claimants that the Prophets and the saints rejoice in being praised, in having eulogies composed and attributed to them, in having their names amplified when mentioned, and in having affairs invented for them alongside Allah, which are not found in the Book of Allah, nor in the Sunnah of His Messenger, nor approved by the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ*), is a bad opinion.

This opinion of the Prophets and the saints is the worst of opinions, because these claimants have likened them in this to the tyrants of this world, whose eyes were covered by the darkness of ignorance before meeting death. It does not come to mind that a tyrant who met death and had the veil lifted from him regarding the command of his Lord in this matter would be content that people exalt him with what Allah did not legislate. How then could it be for the Prophets and the truthful ones?

The word "jah" (standing, rank) that people attach to the prophets and the saints when seeking intercession (tawassul), its customary meaning is authority. Or, if you wish, you may say it is the effectiveness of a word with those over whom one has power or with whom one has standing. So it is said, "So-and-so usurped so-and-so's property through his jah," and "So-and-so freed so-and-so from the punishment for his sin through his jah, with the emir or the vizier, for example." Therefore, if someone claims that a person has jah with Allah in this sense, that is a manifest shirk (associating partners with Allah), not a hidden one. Hardly does the linguistic meaning of the word, which is rank and status, come to the mind of any of those who seek intercession. Moreover, there is no sense in seeking intercession through rank and status themselves, because they are not things that benefit. Such a phrase would have meaning only if it were interpreted as one of the attributes of Allah, such as election (ijtiba') and choosing (istifa'), but these have no connection to supplication, and a supplicant cannot intend them in his prayer. Although al-Alusi (al-Alusi) based the permissibility of seeking intercession through the jah of the Prophet ﷺ specifically on that interpretation, what led him to this was only his fear of the tongues of the common people and the abuse of the ignorant, which has no value in the eyes of the knowledgeable. Thus, seeking intercession with the word jah is a bid'ah (innovation) that arose after the three generations, and it carries the suspicion of shirk, may Allah protect us, and the suspicion of deviating from what the Messenger ﷺ brought. Why, then, the insistence on embellishing this innovation?

Some people say: "We have a proof for this that is no more conclusive than it." It is what al-Tirmidhi narrated with his chain to Uthman ibn Hunayf, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "A blind man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Pray to Allah that He cure me.' He said: 'If you wish, I will pray, and if you wish, you may be patient, and that is better for you.' He said: 'Then pray.' So he commanded him to perform ablution well, and to supplicate with this supplication: 'O Allah, I ask You and turn to You through Your Prophet Muhammad, the Prophet of mercy. O Muhammad! I have turned through you to my Lord regarding this need of mine, that it be fulfilled for me. O Allah, so accept his intercession for me.'" Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hadith that is hasan sahih gharib."

We say first: the hadith has been described as gharib (a report transmitted through a single chain). Moreover, it suffices to require caution in acting upon it that the people of the three generations did not do the like of it, and they knew better than us what must be acted upon in this matter. There is no reason for their abstaining from acting upon it except their knowledge that this belongs to the category of asking a living person to join in supplication, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said in the hadith of seeking rain (istisqa'): "We used to seek intercession (tawassul) to You through our Prophet ﷺ and You gave us rain, and now we seek intercession to You through the uncle of Your Prophet, al-Abbas, so give us rain." He said this, may Allah be pleased with him, while al-Abbas was beside him supplicating to Allah, the Exalted. If tawassul were what these claimants claim, 'Umar would have prayed for rain and sought intercession through the Prophet ﷺ, and would not have said, "We used to seek rain through your Prophet." Asking a person to join in supplication is legislated, even from a brother to his brother, and indeed it may be from the higher to the lower, as has been reported in the hadith. There is nothing in it to fear, for the supplicant and the one who joins him in supplication while he is alive are both servants asking Allah, the Exalted, and the partner in supplication is a partner in servitude, not a vizier who manipulates the will of the emir, as they imagine: "Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe" [Al-Saffat: 180].

Then, the matter falls under the category of creed, not under the category of actions. The question in it returns to this: Is it permissible for us to believe that someone other than Allah may be an intermediary between us and Allah in the fulfillment of our needs, or is it not permissible? As for the Book, it is explicit that this belief is one of the beliefs of the polytheists, and it has disparaged it in His saying: "And they worship besides Allah what neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, 'These are our intercessors with Allah'" [Yunus: 18]. And in the surah we recite every day in prayer: "And You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help" [Al-Fatihah: 5]. So there is no seeking of help except from Him. The Book has also stated explicitly that no one possesses for people any benefit or harm from Allah, and this is the tawhid (monotheism) that was the foundation of the chosen Message, as we have explained.

Then, rational proof guides us that Allah, the Exalted, in His actions is not to be compared to rulers and their likes, who change their will because of what those with standing among them obtain. He is exalted above that, may His majesty be great. If an innovator wished to call to this belief, he must establish for it a proof that leads to certainty, either by rational premises that are demonstrative or by transmitted evidence that is mutawatir (widely transmitted). He cannot take a hadith of solitary transmission (ahad) as evidence for a creed, however strong its chain may be, for it is well known among all the imams that solitary reports yield only conjecture: "And conjecture does not avail against the truth in the least" [An-Najm: 28]. The end of his words, may Allah have mercy on him.

Then I reviewed "Iqtida' al-Sirat al-Mustaqim" (The Straight Path) of the eminent imam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah be pleased with him. I found that he mentioned something similar to that, and his expression is: "The means (wasilah) that Allah commanded seeking encompasses means in His worship and in asking Him. So seeking nearness to Him through the righteous deeds He commanded, and through the supplication and intercession of the prophets and the righteous, is not of the category of swearing by His creatures upon Him. Among this category is the people seeking the intercession of the Prophet ﷺ on the Day of Resurrection, for they ask him to intercede for them with Allah, just as in the world they used to ask him to supplicate for them in seeking rain and other matters. The saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: 'We, when we were afflicted with drought, sought intercession to You through our Prophet, and You gave us rain, and now we seek intercession to You through the uncle of our Prophet,' means: we seek intercession through his supplication, his intercession, and his request. We seek intercession to You through the supplication, request, and intercession of his uncle. It does not mean: 'We swear by him,' or anything that goes in this direction, of what is done after his death and in his absence, as some people say: 'I ask You through the jah of so-and-so with You,' and they say: 'We seek intercession to Allah through His prophets and His saints,' and they narrate a fabricated hadith: 'When you ask Allah, ask Him through my jah, for my jah with Allah is vast.' For if this were the tawassul that the Companions used to do, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned, they would have done it after his death, and they would not have turned away from it to al-Abbas, while knowing that asking by him and swearing by him is greater than al-Abbas. So it is known that the tawassul they mentioned is what is done with the living and not the dead, and it is seeking through their supplication and intercession, for the living is asked for that, while the dead is not asked for anything, neither supplication nor anything else. And likewise the hadith of the blind man: he asked the Prophet ﷺ to supplicate for him so that Allah would restore his sight. The Prophet ﷺ taught him a supplication in which he commanded him to ask Allah to accept his prophet's intercession for him. This indicates that the Prophet ﷺ interceded for him, and commanded him to ask Allah to accept his intercession. And his saying, 'I ask You and turn to You through Your Prophet Muhammad, the Prophet of mercy,' means: through his supplication and his intercession, as 'Umar said: 'We used to seek intercession to You through our Prophet.' So the words 'turning' (tawajjuh) and 'seeking intercession' (tawassul) in the two hadiths have one meaning. Then he said: 'O Muhammad! O Messenger of Allah! I turn through you to my Lord regarding my need, that He may fulfill it. O Allah, so accept his intercession for me.' So he asked Allah to accept the intercession of His Prophet for him. As for his saying: 'O Muhammad! O Prophet of Allah!' this and its like is a call (nida'), by which one seeks to summon the one called upon into the heart, (p-4922) so he addresses in the heart the one who is witnessed, as the worshipper says: 'Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings.' A person does this often, addressing whoever he imagines in his mind, even if there is no one outside to hear the address. So the expression of seeking intercession through a person, turning through him, and asking through him, contains generality and ambiguity, and it is an error whose cause is one who did not understand the intent of the Companions. It may mean clinging to him (originally, causing a means through him), because he is a supplicant and intercessor, for example, or because the supplicant is beloved to him, obedient to his command, and follows his example. So the causation is either through the asker's love for him and his following of him, or through the supplication and intercession of the means. And it may mean swearing by him and seeking intercession through his very person, so that the tawassul is not through any action of his nor any action of the asker, but through his person or merely by swearing by him upon Allah. This last is what they disliked and forbade." The end of his words.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 33, verses 64–69 (part 1 of 2)**

**On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[64–66] ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein forever, they will find no protector or helper.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 65] ﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire, they will say, "Oh, would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 66]

﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers﴾, i.e., He has removed them far from His mercy. ﴿And prepared for them a blaze﴾, i.e., a Fire of intense burning in the Hereafter. ﴿Abiding therein forever, they will find no protector﴾ [al-Ahzab: 65], i.e., no guardian who takes charge of them. ﴿Or helper﴾ [al-Ahzab: 65], i.e., one who rescues them. ﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire﴾ [al-Ahzab: 66], i.e., they are turned about from one side to another, likened to a piece of meat in a boiling pot, which the boiling tosses from one side to the other. Or the meaning is: from one state to another, so what is intended is the change of their forms, from blackness and shriveling and other such conditions.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The faces are singled out for mention because the face is the most honored part of a human being's body. It is also permissible for "the face" to be an expression for the whole person. The verb governing the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) may be "they will say," or "remember," or "they will not find," or "abiding," or "helper." ﴿They will say, "Oh, would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 66], i.e., then we would have been saved from this punishment.

[67–69] ﴿And they will say, "Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our leaders and our elders, and they misled us from the way."﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67] ﴿"Our Lord, give them double the punishment and curse them with a great cursing."﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68] ﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who abused Moses, but Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honored in the sight of Allah.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69]

﴿And they will say, "Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our leaders and our elders"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]. These are the leaders of disbelief, who instilled disbelief in them and made it appealing to them until they imitated them in it. ﴿And they misled us from the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67], i.e., by what they had made appealing to us. Al-Zamakhshari said: The addition of the alif for the prolongation of the sound makes the verse-endings like the rhymes of poetry. Its function is pausing, and indicating that the speech has ended and what follows it is a new statement. ﴿"Our Lord, give them double the punishment"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68], i.e., twice the punishment You gave us, because they went astray and led others astray. ﴿And curse them with a great cursing﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68], i.e., a cursing that is the most intense and the greatest of curses.

It is also recited as "kathīran" (many), meaning a multiplicity of the numbers of curses.

﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who abused Moses, but Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honored in the sight of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69]. When Almighty Allah explained the threat against whoever harms His Prophet ﷺ, that he deserves the curse in both abodes, He alluded to those among them who had uttered something of harm in the story of Zayd and Zaynab, for which the surah was revealed. He also concluded it with the instruction to keep far from resembling a people who harmed Moses, peace be upon him, by belittling him at times, showing lack of courtesy toward him at other times, and attributing to him at still other times things that contradict the prophetic mission. Much of this passes before the readers of their Torah, which indicates that they did not fulfill his mission and prophethood their due, in terms of honoring him, sending blessings upon him, and submitting to his command and judgment. So the result was that Allah became angry with them, struck them with various kinds of punishments, and disgrace befell them. He cleared His Messenger Moses, peace be upon him, of their slander, and exalted his station above their belittling, by affirming his excellence, raising his rank, and granting him ​​wajāha, which means greatness and nearness, in His sight.

Thus the word of curse and humiliation was fulfilled upon those who harmed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and destruction overtook them. He expanded the breast of His Prophet, raised his mention, elevated his rank, and magnified his standing, for as long as the eras succeed one another.

Close to this verse in meaning and allusion is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And [mention] when Moses said to his people, "O my people, why do you harm me while you know that I am the messenger of Allah to you?" So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate, and Allah does not guide the defiant people.﴾ [al-Saff: 5] In both verses there is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ, in that he follows the example of his brother Moses, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them both. The Prophet ﷺ often used to say, in reply to the rude Bedouins when something displeasing reached him or he heard it: "May the mercy of Allah be upon Moses; he was harmed with more than this and was patient."

The commentators have related reports here, the best of which is what al-Bazzar narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "Moses was a modest man, and he came to the water to bathe. He placed his garments on a rock, and his private parts were hardly ever seen. The Children of Israel said, 'Moses is ādar' (has a swelling of the testicles) or he has some defect,' meaning that he does not take off his garments. So the rock carried off his garments until it came to a place in front of the Children of Israel, and they looked at Moses and saw him as the most handsome of men, or as he said." That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿But Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honored in the sight of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69]. Al-Bukhari also narrated it in his Sahih from Abu Hurayrah.

Al-Razi said: The hadith about the harming of Moses is subject to differing opinions, i.e., because of the multiplicity of narrations about it. Moreover, the harm mentioned in the Qur'an is sufficient, such as their saying: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24], and their saying: ﴿We will never believe you until we see Allah outright﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55], and their saying: ﴿We will never endure one kind of food﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61], and so on. So He said to the believers: "Do not be like them." End of quote.

Ibn Kathir said: It is possible that all that has been narrated is intended, and that there is other besides it. End of quote. That is, because of the generality of the implied object. What we have explained first is the closer to the meaning. And Allah knows best.

**First:** *al-Wajīh* (the dignified one), linguistically, has the meaning of "the lord," like *al-wajh* (the face). One says: "These are the faces of the town and its dignitaries," i.e., its nobles. It also means "the one possessing status" (*dhū al-jāh*). *Al-jāh* means rank and position, and it is an inverted form of *wajh*: when the *wāw* was moved to the place of the *ʿayn* and it became *jawah*, the *wāw* was changed into an *alif*, so it became *jāh*. The same is stated in al-Qamus and its commentary.

Therefore he used to ward off accusations from him, repel harm, and guard him, so that no defect would reach him and he would not be described with any deficiency, just as a king does with one who has closeness and standing with him. Thus, seeking intercession with the word jah is a bid'ah (innovation) that arose after the three generations, and it carries the suspicion of shirk, may Allah protect us, and the suspicion of deviating from what the Messenger ﷺ brought. Why, then, the insistence on embellishing this innovation?

Some people say: "We have a proof for this that is no more conclusive than it." It is what al-Tirmidhi narrated with his chain to Uthman ibn Hunayf, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "A blind man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Pray to Allah that He cure me.' He said: 'If you wish, I will pray, and if you wish, you may be patient, and that is better for you.' He said: 'Then pray.' So he commanded him to perform ablution well, and to supplicate with this supplication: 'O Allah, I ask You and turn to You through Your Prophet Muhammad, the Prophet of mercy. O Muhammad! I have turned through you to my Lord regarding this need of mine, that it be fulfilled for me. O Allah, so accept his intercession for me.'" Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hadith that is hasan sahih gharib."

We say first: the hadith has been described as gharib (a report transmitted through a single chain). Moreover, it suffices to require caution in acting upon it that the people of the three generations did not do the like of it, and they knew better than us what must be acted upon in this matter. There is no reason for their abstaining from acting upon it except their knowledge that this belongs to the category of asking a living person to join in supplication, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said in the hadith of seeking rain (istisqa'): "We used to seek intercession (tawassul) to You through our Prophet ﷺ and You gave us rain, and now we seek intercession to You through the uncle of Your Prophet, al-Abbas, so give us rain." He said this, may Allah be pleased with him, while al-Abbas was beside him supplicating to Allah, the Exalted. If tawassul were what these claimants claim, 'Umar would have prayed for rain and sought intercession through the Prophet ﷺ, and would not have said, "We used to seek rain through your Prophet." Asking a person to join in supplication is legislated, even from a brother to his brother, and indeed it may be from the higher to the lower, as has been reported in the hadith. There is nothing in it to fear, for the supplicant and the one who joins him in supplication while he is alive are both servants asking Allah, the Exalted, and the partner in supplication is a partner in servitude, not a vizier who manipulates the will of the emir, as they imagine: "Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe" [Al-Saffat: 180].

Then, the matter falls under the category of creed, not under the category of actions. The question in it returns to this: Is it permissible for us to believe that someone other than Allah may be an intermediary between us and Allah in the fulfillment of our needs, or is it not permissible? As for the Book, it is explicit that this belief is one of the beliefs of the polytheists, and it has disparaged it in His saying: "And they worship besides Allah what neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, 'These are our intercessors with Allah'" [Yunus: 18]. And in the surah we recite every day in prayer: "And You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help" [Al-Fatihah: 5]. So there is no seeking of help except from Him. The Book has also stated explicitly that no one possesses for people any benefit or harm from Allah, and this is the tawhid (monotheism) that was the foundation of the chosen Message, as we have explained.

Then, rational proof guides us that Allah, the Exalted, in His actions is not to be compared to rulers and their likes, who change their will because of what those with standing among them obtain. He is exalted above that, may His majesty be great. If an innovator wished to call to this belief, he must establish for it a proof that leads to certainty, either by rational premises that are demonstrative or by transmitted evidence that is mutawatir (widely transmitted). He cannot take a hadith of solitary transmission (ahad) as evidence for a creed, however strong its chain may be, for it is well known among all the imams that solitary reports yield only conjecture: "And conjecture does not avail against the truth in the least" [An-Najm: 28]. The end of his words, may Allah have mercy on him.

Then I reviewed "Iqtida' al-Sirat al-Mustaqim" (The Straight Path) of the eminent imam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah be pleased with him. I found that he mentioned something similar to that, and his expression is: "The means (wasilah) that Allah commanded seeking encompasses means in His worship and in asking Him. So seeking nearness to Him through the righteous deeds He commanded, and through the supplication and intercession of the prophets and the righteous, is not of the category of swearing by His creatures upon Him. Among this category is the people seeking the intercession of the Prophet ﷺ on the Day of Resurrection, for they ask him to intercede for them with Allah, just as in the world they used to ask him to supplicate for them in seeking rain and other matters. The saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: 'We, when we were afflicted with drought, sought intercession to You through our Prophet, and You gave us rain, and now we seek intercession to You through the uncle of our Prophet,' means: we seek intercession through his supplication, his intercession, and his request. We seek intercession to You through the supplication, request, and intercession of his uncle. It does not mean: 'We swear by him,' or anything that goes in this direction, of what is done after his death and in his absence, as some people say: 'I ask You through the jah of so-and-so with You,' and they say: 'We seek intercession to Allah through His prophets and His saints,' and they narrate a fabricated hadith: 'When you ask Allah, ask Him through my jah, for my jah with Allah is vast.' For if this were the tawassul that the Companions used to do, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned, they would have done it after his death, and they would not have turned away from it to al-Abbas, while knowing that asking by him and swearing by him is greater than al-Abbas. So it is known that the tawassul they mentioned is what is done with the living and not the dead, and it is seeking through their supplication and intercession, for the living is asked for that, while the dead is not asked for anything, neither supplication nor anything else. And likewise the hadith of the blind man: he asked the Prophet ﷺ to supplicate for him so that Allah would restore his sight. The Prophet ﷺ taught him a supplication in which he commanded him to ask Allah to accept his prophet's intercession for him. This indicates that the Prophet ﷺ interceded for him, and commanded him to ask Allah to accept his intercession. And his saying, 'I ask You and turn to You through Your Prophet Muhammad, the Prophet of mercy,' means: through his supplication and his intercession, as 'Umar said: 'We used to seek intercession to You through our Prophet.' So the words 'turning' (tawajjuh) and 'seeking intercession' (tawassul) in the two hadiths have one meaning. Then he said: 'O Muhammad! O Messenger of Allah! I turn through you to my Lord regarding my need, that He may fulfill it. O Allah, so accept his intercession for me.' So he asked Allah to accept the intercession of His Prophet for him. As for his saying: 'O Muhammad! O Prophet of Allah!' this and its like is a call (nida'), by which one seeks to summon the one called upon into the heart, (p-4922) so he addresses in the heart the one who is witnessed, as the worshipper says: 'Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings.' A person does this often, addressing whoever he imagines in his mind, even if there is no one outside to hear the address. So the expression of seeking intercession through a person, turning through him, and asking through him, contains generality and ambiguity, and it is an error whose cause is one who did not understand the intent of the Companions. It may mean clinging to him (originally, causing a means through him), because he is a supplicant and intercessor, for example, or because the supplicant is beloved to him, obedient to his command, and follows his example. So the causation is either through the asker's love for him and his following of him, or through the supplication and intercession of the means. And it may mean swearing by him and seeking intercession through his very person, so that the tawassul is not through any action of his nor any action of the asker, but through his person or merely by swearing by him upon Allah. This last is what they disliked and forbade." The end of his words.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 33, verses 64–69 (part 1 of 2)**

**On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[64–66] ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein forever, they will find no protector or helper.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 65] ﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire, they will say, "Oh, would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 66]

﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers﴾, i.e., He has removed them far from His mercy. ﴿And prepared for them a blaze﴾, i.e., a Fire of intense burning in the Hereafter. ﴿Abiding therein forever, they will find no protector﴾ [al-Ahzab: 65], i.e., no guardian who takes charge of them. ﴿Or helper﴾ [al-Ahzab: 65], i.e., one who rescues them. ﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire﴾ [al-Ahzab: 66], i.e., they are turned about from one side to another, likened to a piece of meat in a boiling pot, which the boiling tosses from one side to the other. Or the meaning is: from one state to another, so what is intended is the change of their forms, from blackness and shriveling and other such conditions.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The faces are singled out for mention because the face is the most honored part of a human being's body. It is also permissible for "the face" to be an expression for the whole person. The verb governing the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) may be "they will say," or "remember," or "they will not find," or "abiding," or "helper." ﴿They will say, "Oh, would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 66], i.e., then we would have been saved from this punishment.

[67–69] ﴿And they will say, "Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our leaders and our elders, and they misled us from the way."﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67] ﴿"Our Lord, give them double the punishment and curse them with a great cursing."﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68] ﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who abused Moses, but Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honored in the sight of Allah.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69]

﴿And they will say, "Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our leaders and our elders"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]. These are the leaders of disbelief, who instilled disbelief in them and made it appealing to them until they imitated them in it. ﴿And they misled us from the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67], i.e., by what they had made appealing to us. Al-Zamakhshari said: The addition of the alif for the prolongation of the sound makes the verse-endings like the rhymes of poetry. Its function is pausing, and indicating that the speech has ended and what follows it is a new statement. ﴿"Our Lord, give them double the punishment"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68], i.e., twice the punishment You gave us, because they went astray and led others astray. ﴿And curse them with a great cursing﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68], i.e., a cursing that is the most intense and the greatest of curses.

It is also recited as "kathīran" (many), meaning a multiplicity of the numbers of curses.

﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who abused Moses, but Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honored in the sight of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69]. When Almighty Allah explained the threat against whoever harms His Prophet ﷺ, that he deserves the curse in both abodes, He alluded to those among them who had uttered something of harm in the story of Zayd and Zaynab, for which the surah was revealed. He also concluded it with the instruction to keep far from resembling a people who harmed Moses, peace be upon him, by belittling him at times, showing lack of courtesy toward him at other times, and attributing to him at still other times things that contradict the prophetic mission. Much of this passes before the readers of their Torah, which indicates that they did not fulfill his mission and prophethood their due, in terms of honoring him, sending blessings upon him, and submitting to his command and judgment. So the result was that Allah became angry with them, struck them with various kinds of punishments, and disgrace befell them. He cleared His Messenger Moses, peace be upon him, of their slander, and exalted his station above their belittling, by affirming his excellence, raising his rank, and granting him ​​wajāha, which means greatness and nearness, in His sight.

Thus the word of curse and humiliation was fulfilled upon those who harmed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and destruction overtook them. He expanded the breast of His Prophet, raised his mention, elevated his rank, and magnified his standing, for as long as the eras succeed one another.

Close to this verse in meaning and allusion is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And [mention] when Moses said to his people, "O my people, why do you harm me while you know that I am the messenger of Allah to you?" So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate, and Allah does not guide the defiant people.﴾ [al-Saff: 5] In both verses there is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ, in that he follows the example of his brother Moses, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them both. The Prophet ﷺ often used to say, in reply to the rude Bedouins when something displeasing reached him or he heard it: "May the mercy of Allah be upon Moses; he was harmed with more than this and was patient."

The commentators have related reports here, the best of which is what al-Bazzar narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "Moses was a modest man, and he came to the water to bathe. He placed his garments on a rock, and his private parts were hardly ever seen. The Children of Israel said, 'Moses is ādar' (has a swelling of the testicles) or he has some defect,' meaning that he does not take off his garments. So the rock carried off his garments until it came to a place in front of the Children of Israel, and they looked at Moses and saw him as the most handsome of men, or as he said." That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿But Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honored in the sight of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69]. Al-Bukhari also narrated it in his Sahih from Abu Hurayrah.

Al-Razi said: The hadith about the harming of Moses is subject to differing opinions, i.e., because of the multiplicity of narrations about it. Moreover, the harm mentioned in the Qur'an is sufficient, such as their saying: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24], and their saying: ﴿We will never believe you until we see Allah outright﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55], and their saying: ﴿We will never endure one kind of food﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61], and so on. So He said to the believers: "Do not be like them." End of quote.

Ibn Kathir said: It is possible that all that has been narrated is intended, and that there is other besides it. End of quote. That is, because of the generality of the implied object. What we have explained first is the closer to the meaning. And Allah knows best.

**Remarks:**

**First:** *al-Wajīh* (the dignified one), linguistically, has the meaning of "the lord," like *al-wajh* (the face). One says: "These are the faces of the town and its dignitaries," i.e., its nobles. It also means "the one possessing status" (*dhū al-jāh*). *Al-jāh* means rank and position, and it is an inverted form of *wajh*: when the *wāw* was moved to the place of the *ʿayn* and it became *jawah*, the *wāw* was changed into an *alif*, so it became *jāh*. The same is stated in al-Qamus and its commentary.

**Second:** Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Wajīhan*" means possessing status and rank with Him. Therefore he used to ward off accusations from him, repel harm, and guard him, so that no defect would reach him and he would not be described with any deficiency, just as a king does with one who has closeness and standing with him. Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said: That is, Moses was one whose intercession with Allah was accepted in what he asked, having face and rank with Him through his obedience to Him; that is, he was accepted and granted what he requested from Allah, the Exalted, for his people, out of Allah's favor and preference toward him.

**Third:** The common people, and many of those who pose as scholars, have taken the attribute of *wajāha* (standing) for the Prophets as a means of requesting and seeking from them, which does not fit reason or transmission, nor does it correspond to the linguistic meaning in any way. The Imam, Shaykh Muhammad ʿAbduh, may God have mercy on him, wrote a legal opinion on this matter, clarifying the correct position regarding what is ambiguous in this issue. He was asked, may God have mercy on him, about one who seeks intercession through the Prophets and the saints, believing that the Prophet or the saint can sway the will of Allah Exalted from what it is, as is commonly understood among people regarding the meaning of intercession and standing before a ruler, and that seeking intercession through them to Allah Exalted is like seeking intercession through notable people to rulers.

One man said: This undermines the creed; comparing seeking intercession with Allah Exalted to seeking intercession with rulers is impossible. The creed of monotheism (*tawḥīd*) is that there is no doer, no benefiter, and no harmer except Allah Exalted, and that none is invoked alongside Him, as He Exalted said: ﴿So do not invoke anyone with Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. And the Prophet ﷺ, although he is the most exalted in rank with Allah Exalted of all mankind, the greatest of people in standing and love, and the nearest to Him, has no part in the affair, and does not possess for people any harm, benefit, guidance, or anything else, as is stated in the text of the Qur'an.

He is only a conveyor of the message from Allah Exalted, and one does not draw near to Allah Exalted except by acting upon what came through his tongue ﷺ, and following what the Companions, the Successors, and the rightly-guided imams who exercised independent judgment followed of his guidance and sunnah. There is no means for bringing benefits and warding off harms except what Allah has guided people to. There is no meaning to seeking intercession through a Prophet or a saint except by following him and emulating him. Many verses revealed in the Mighty Qur'an guide us to this, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31] ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153], and others besides these verses. If this is the correct position, I hope to have it confirmed in writing, so that I may defend myself against one who has thought ill of me.

He, may God have mercy on him, replied after the basmala and the hawqala: Your belief is this, and it is the correct belief, with no admixture of error, and it is what every Muslim who believes in what Muhammad ﷺ brought must hold; for the foundation upon which the mission of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ grows is this meaning of monotheism, as Allah said: ﴿Say, He is Allah, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1] ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2]. *Al-Samad* is the one who is turned to in needs, and to whom those who nurture (others) turn for help in what they seek, and for strength when their own powers fail. Expressing the predicate in this form conveys restriction (*ḥaṣr*), as is known among the people of the language; so there is no *samad* except Him.

He has guided us to the obligation of directing oneself to Him alone in the clearest expression, in His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186]. Shaykh Muhyi al-Din Ibn al-ʿArabi, the shaykh of the Sufis, said on page 226 of the fourth volume of his *al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya*, in discussing this verse: Indeed, Allah Exalted has not left a proof for His servant against Him. Rather, the conclusive proof belongs to Allah. So one does not seek nearness to Him through anything other than Him, for seeking nearness is only the pursuit of closeness to Him, and Allah has informed us that He is near, and His report is true. End of quote, summarized.

Moreover, those who claim the permissibility of some of what the common people do today in this matter only speak about it in vague terms, and they follow paths of interpretation that do not correspond to what is in people's hearts. They interpret *jāh* and *wāsiṭah* (intermediary) in ways that have no effect on the imaginations of those who hold the belief. What state would compel them to this? Before them are the first three generations, and there was none of this seeking of intercession in them, nor anything resembling it in any way. The books of the Sunnah and the biographies are before us as witnesses to this. Everything that came into being after that is, at the least of its descriptions, a *bidʿah* (innovation) in religion, and every innovation is misguidance, and every misguidance is in the Fire.

The worst of innovations is that in which there is a semblance of associating partners with Allah Exalted and of having ill opinion of Him, such as these innovations we are discussing. It seems to these claimants that this is an exaltation of the status of the Prophet ﷺ, or of the Prophets, or of the saints, although the best exaltation of the Prophets is to stop at what they brought, and to avoid adding to what they legislated by the permission of their Lord. The exaltation of the saints is by choosing what they chose for themselves. The thought of these claimants that the Prophets and the saints rejoice in being praised, in having eulogies composed and attributed to them, in having their names amplified when mentioned, and in having affairs invented for them alongside Allah, which are not found in the Book of Allah, nor in the Sunnah of His Messenger, nor approved by the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ*), is a bad opinion.

This opinion of the Prophets and the saints is the worst of opinions, because these claimants have likened them in this to the tyrants of this world, whose eyes were covered by the darkness of ignorance before meeting death. It does not come to mind that a tyrant who met death and had the veil lifted from him regarding the command of his Lord in this matter would be content that people exalt him with what Allah did not legislate. How then could it be for the Prophets and the truthful ones?

The word "jah" (standing, rank) that people attach to the prophets and the saints when seeking intercession (tawassul), its customary meaning is authority. Or, if you wish, you may say it is the effectiveness of a word with those over whom one has power or with whom one has standing. So it is said, "So-and-so usurped so-and-so's property through his jah," and "So-and-so freed so-and-so from the punishment for his sin through his jah, with the emir or the vizier, for example." Therefore, if someone claims that a person has jah with Allah in this sense, that is a manifest shirk (associating partners with Allah), not a hidden one. Hardly does the linguistic meaning of the word, which is rank and status, come to the mind of any of those who seek intercession. Moreover, there is no sense in seeking intercession through rank and status themselves, because they are not things that benefit. Such a phrase would have meaning only if it were interpreted as one of the attributes of Allah, such as election (ijtiba') and choosing (istifa'), but these have no connection to supplication, and a supplicant cannot intend them in his prayer. Thus, seeking intercession with the word jah is a bid'ah (innovation) that arose after the three generations, and it carries the suspicion of shirk, may Allah protect us, and the suspicion of deviating from what the Messenger ﷺ brought. He said: 'If you wish, I will pray, and if you wish, you may be patient, and that is better for you.' He said: 'Then pray.' He said this, may Allah be pleased with him, while al-Abbas was beside him supplicating to Allah, the Exalted. If tawassul were what these claimants claim, 'Umar would have prayed for rain and sought intercession through the Prophet ﷺ, and would not have said, "We used to seek rain through your Prophet." Asking a person to join in supplication is legislated, even from a brother to his brother, and indeed it may be from the higher to the lower, as has been reported in the hadith. And in the surah we recite every day in prayer: "And You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help" [Al-Fatihah: 5]. So there is no seeking of help except from Him. The Book has also stated explicitly that no one possesses for people any benefit or harm from Allah, and this is the tawhid (monotheism) that was the foundation of the chosen Message, as we have explained.

The end of his words, may Allah have mercy on him.

Then I reviewed "Iqtida' al-Sirat al-Mustaqim" (The Straight Path) of the eminent imam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah be pleased with him. I found that he mentioned something similar to that, and his expression is: "The means (wasilah) that Allah commanded seeking encompasses means in His worship and in asking Him. So seeking nearness to Him through the righteous deeds He commanded, and through the supplication and intercession of the prophets and the righteous, is not of the category of swearing by His creatures upon Him. Among this category is the people seeking the intercession of the Prophet ﷺ on the Day of Resurrection, for they ask him to intercede for them with Allah, just as in the world they used to ask him to supplicate for them in seeking rain and other matters.
