We seek intercession to You through the supplication, request, and intercession of his uncle. It does not mean: 'We swear by him,' or anything that goes in this direction, of what is done after his death and in his absence, as some people say: 'I ask You through the jah of so-and-so with You,' and they say: 'We seek intercession to Allah through His prophets and His saints,' and they narrate a fabricated hadith: 'When you ask Allah, ask Him through my jah, for my jah with Allah is vast.' For if this were the tawassul that the Companions used to do, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned, they would have done it after his death, and they would not have turned away from it to al-Abbas, while knowing that asking by him and swearing by him is greater than al-Abbas. So it is known that the tawassul they mentioned is what is done with the living and not the dead, and it is seeking through their supplication and intercession, for the living is asked for that, while the dead is not asked for anything, neither supplication nor anything else. And likewise the hadith of the blind man: he asked the Prophet ﷺ to supplicate for him so that Allah would restore his sight. The Prophet ﷺ taught him a supplication in which he commanded him to ask Allah to accept his prophet's intercession for him. This indicates that the Prophet ﷺ interceded for him, and commanded him to ask Allah to accept his intercession. And his saying, 'I ask You and turn to You through Your Prophet Muhammad, the Prophet of mercy,' means: through his supplication and his intercession, as 'Umar said: 'We used to seek intercession to You through our Prophet.' So the words 'turning' (tawajjuh) and 'seeking intercession' (tawassul) in the two hadiths have one meaning. Then he said: 'O Muhammad! O Messenger of Allah! I turn through you to my Lord regarding my need, that He may fulfill it. O Allah, so accept his intercession for me.' So he asked Allah to accept the intercession of His Prophet for him. As for his saying: 'O Muhammad! O Prophet of Allah!' this and its like is a call (nida'), by which one seeks to summon the one called upon into the heart, (p-4922) so he addresses in the heart the one who is witnessed, as the worshipper says: 'Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings.' A person does this often, addressing whoever he imagines in his mind, even if there is no one outside to hear the address. So the expression of seeking intercession through a person, turning through him, and asking through him, contains generality and ambiguity, and it is an error whose cause is one who did not understand the intent of the Companions. It may mean clinging to him (originally, causing a means through him), because he is a supplicant and intercessor, for example, or because the supplicant is beloved to him, obedient to his command, and follows his example. So the causation is either through the asker's love for him and his following of him, or through the supplication and intercession of the means. And it may mean swearing by him and seeking intercession through his very person, so that the tawassul is not through any action of his nor any action of the asker, but through his person or merely by swearing by him upon Allah. This last is what they disliked and forbade." The end of his words.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 33, verses 64–69 (part 1 of 2)**

**On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[64–66] ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein forever, they will find no protector or helper.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 65] ﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire, they will say, "Oh, would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 66]

﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers﴾, i.e., He has removed them far from His mercy. ﴿And prepared for them a blaze﴾, i.e., a Fire of intense burning in the Hereafter. ﴿Abiding therein forever, they will find no protector﴾ [al-Ahzab: 65], i.e., no guardian who takes charge of them. ﴿Or helper﴾ [al-Ahzab: 65], i.e., one who rescues them. ﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire﴾ [al-Ahzab: 66], i.e., they are turned about from one side to another, likened to a piece of meat in a boiling pot, which the boiling tosses from one side to the other. Or the meaning is: from one state to another, so what is intended is the change of their forms, from blackness and shriveling and other such conditions.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The faces are singled out for mention because the face is the most honored part of a human being's body. It is also permissible for "the face" to be an expression for the whole person. The verb governing the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) may be "they will say," or "remember," or "they will not find," or "abiding," or "helper." ﴿They will say, "Oh, would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 66], i.e., then we would have been saved from this punishment.

[67–69] ﴿And they will say, "Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our leaders and our elders, and they misled us from the way."﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67] ﴿"Our Lord, give them double the punishment and curse them with a great cursing."﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68] ﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who abused Moses, but Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honored in the sight of Allah.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69]

﴿And they will say, "Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our leaders and our elders"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]. These are the leaders of disbelief, who instilled disbelief in them and made it appealing to them until they imitated them in it. ﴿And they misled us from the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67], i.e., by what they had made appealing to us. Al-Zamakhshari said: The addition of the alif for the prolongation of the sound makes the verse-endings like the rhymes of poetry. Its function is pausing, and indicating that the speech has ended and what follows it is a new statement. ﴿"Our Lord, give them double the punishment"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68], i.e., twice the punishment You gave us, because they went astray and led others astray. ﴿And curse them with a great cursing﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68], i.e., a cursing that is the most intense and the greatest of curses.

It is also recited as "kathīran" (many), meaning a multiplicity of the numbers of curses.

﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who abused Moses, but Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honored in the sight of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69]. When Almighty Allah explained the threat against whoever harms His Prophet ﷺ, that he deserves the curse in both abodes, He alluded to those among them who had uttered something of harm in the story of Zayd and Zaynab, for which the surah was revealed. He also concluded it with the instruction to keep far from resembling a people who harmed Moses, peace be upon him, by belittling him at times, showing lack of courtesy toward him at other times, and attributing to him at still other times things that contradict the prophetic mission. Much of this passes before the readers of their Torah, which indicates that they did not fulfill his mission and prophethood their due, in terms of honoring him, sending blessings upon him, and submitting to his command and judgment. So the result was that Allah became angry with them, struck them with various kinds of punishments, and disgrace befell them. He cleared His Messenger Moses, peace be upon him, of their slander, and exalted his station above their belittling, by affirming his excellence, raising his rank, and granting him ​​wajāha, which means greatness and nearness, in His sight.

Thus the word of curse and humiliation was fulfilled upon those who harmed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and destruction overtook them. He expanded the breast of His Prophet, raised his mention, elevated his rank, and magnified his standing, for as long as the eras succeed one another.

Close to this verse in meaning and allusion is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And [mention] when Moses said to his people, "O my people, why do you harm me while you know that I am the messenger of Allah to you?" So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate, and Allah does not guide the defiant people.﴾ [al-Saff: 5] In both verses there is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ, in that he follows the example of his brother Moses, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them both. The Prophet ﷺ often used to say, in reply to the rude Bedouins when something displeasing reached him or he heard it: "May the mercy of Allah be upon Moses; he was harmed with more than this and was patient."

The commentators have related reports here, the best of which is what al-Bazzar narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "Moses was a modest man, and he came to the water to bathe. He placed his garments on a rock, and his private parts were hardly ever seen. The Children of Israel said, 'Moses is ādar' (has a swelling of the testicles) or he has some defect,' meaning that he does not take off his garments. So the rock carried off his garments until it came to a place in front of the Children of Israel, and they looked at Moses and saw him as the most handsome of men, or as he said." That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿But Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honored in the sight of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69]. Al-Bukhari also narrated it in his Sahih from Abu Hurayrah.

Al-Razi said: The hadith about the harming of Moses is subject to differing opinions, i.e., because of the multiplicity of narrations about it. Moreover, the harm mentioned in the Qur'an is sufficient, such as their saying: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24], and their saying: ﴿We will never believe you until we see Allah outright﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55], and their saying: ﴿We will never endure one kind of food﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61], and so on. So He said to the believers: "Do not be like them." End of quote.

Ibn Kathir said: It is possible that all that has been narrated is intended, and that there is other besides it. End of quote. That is, because of the generality of the implied object. What we have explained first is the closer to the meaning. And Allah knows best.

**Remarks:**

**First:** *al-Wajīh* (the dignified one), linguistically, has the meaning of "the lord," like *al-wajh* (the face). One says: "These are the faces of the town and its dignitaries," i.e., its nobles. It also means "the one possessing status" (*dhū al-jāh*). *Al-jāh* means rank and position, and it is an inverted form of *wajh*: when the *wāw* was moved to the place of the *ʿayn* and it became *jawah*, the *wāw* was changed into an *alif*, so it became *jāh*. The same is stated in al-Qamus and its commentary.

**Second:** Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Wajīhan*" means possessing status and rank with Him. Therefore he used to ward off accusations from him, repel harm, and guard him, so that no defect would reach him and he would not be described with any deficiency, just as a king does with one who has closeness and standing with him. Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said: That is, Moses was one whose intercession with Allah was accepted in what he asked, having face and rank with Him through his obedience to Him; that is, he was accepted and granted what he requested from Allah, the Exalted, for his people, out of Allah's favor and preference toward him.

**Third:** The common people, and many of those who pose as scholars, have taken the attribute of *wajāha* (standing) for the Prophets as a means of requesting and seeking from them, which does not fit reason or transmission, nor does it correspond to the linguistic meaning in any way. The Imam, Shaykh Muhammad ʿAbduh, may God have mercy on him, wrote a legal opinion on this matter, clarifying the correct position regarding what is ambiguous in this issue. He was asked, may God have mercy on him, about one who seeks intercession through the Prophets and the saints, believing that the Prophet or the saint can sway the will of Allah Exalted from what it is, as is commonly understood among people regarding the meaning of intercession and standing before a ruler, and that seeking intercession through them to Allah Exalted is like seeking intercession through notable people to rulers.

One man said: This undermines the creed; comparing seeking intercession with Allah Exalted to seeking intercession with rulers is impossible. The creed of monotheism (*tawḥīd*) is that there is no doer, no benefiter, and no harmer except Allah Exalted, and that none is invoked alongside Him, as He Exalted said: ﴿So do not invoke anyone with Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. And the Prophet ﷺ, although he is the most exalted in rank with Allah Exalted of all mankind, the greatest of people in standing and love, and the nearest to Him, has no part in the affair, and does not possess for people any harm, benefit, guidance, or anything else, as is stated in the text of the Qur'an.

He is only a conveyor of the message from Allah Exalted, and one does not draw near to Allah Exalted except by acting upon what came through his tongue ﷺ, and following what the Companions, the Successors, and the rightly-guided imams who exercised independent judgment followed of his guidance and sunnah. There is no means for bringing benefits and warding off harms except what Allah has guided people to. There is no meaning to seeking intercession through a Prophet or a saint except by following him and emulating him. Many verses revealed in the Mighty Qur'an guide us to this, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31] ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153], and others besides these verses. If this is the correct position, I hope to have it confirmed in writing, so that I may defend myself against one who has thought ill of me.

He, may God have mercy on him, replied after the basmala and the hawqala: Your belief is this, and it is the correct belief, with no admixture of error, and it is what every Muslim who believes in what Muhammad ﷺ brought must hold; for the foundation upon which the mission of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ grows is this meaning of monotheism, as Allah said: ﴿Say, He is Allah, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1] ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2]. *Al-Samad* is the one who is turned to in needs, and to whom those who nurture (others) turn for help in what they seek, and for strength when their own powers fail. Expressing the predicate in this form conveys restriction (*ḥaṣr*), as is known among the people of the language; so there is no *samad* except Him.

He has guided us to the obligation of directing oneself to Him alone in the clearest expression, in His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186]. Shaykh Muhyi al-Din Ibn al-ʿArabi, the shaykh of the Sufis, said on page 226 of the fourth volume of his *al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya*, in discussing this verse: Indeed, Allah Exalted has not left a proof for His servant against Him. Rather, the conclusive proof belongs to Allah. So one does not seek nearness to Him through anything other than Him, for seeking nearness is only the pursuit of closeness to Him, and Allah has informed us that He is near, and His report is true. End of quote, summarized.

Moreover, those who claim the permissibility of some of what the common people do today in this matter only speak about it in vague terms, and they follow paths of interpretation that do not correspond to what is in people's hearts. They interpret *jāh* and *wāsiṭah* (intermediary) in ways that have no effect on the imaginations of those who hold the belief. What state would compel them to this? Before them are the first three generations, and there was none of this seeking of intercession in them, nor anything resembling it in any way. The books of the Sunnah and the biographies are before us as witnesses to this. Everything that came into being after that is, at the least of its descriptions, a *bidʿah* (innovation) in religion, and every innovation is misguidance, and every misguidance is in the Fire.

The worst of innovations is that in which there is a semblance of associating partners with Allah Exalted and of having ill opinion of Him, such as these innovations we are discussing. It seems to these claimants that this is an exaltation of the status of the Prophet ﷺ, or of the Prophets, or of the saints, although the best exaltation of the Prophets is to stop at what they brought, and to avoid adding to what they legislated by the permission of their Lord. The exaltation of the saints is by choosing what they chose for themselves. The thought of these claimants that the Prophets and the saints rejoice in being praised, in having eulogies composed and attributed to them, in having their names amplified when mentioned, and in having affairs invented for them alongside Allah, which are not found in the Book of Allah, nor in the Sunnah of His Messenger, nor approved by the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ*), is a bad opinion.

This opinion of the Prophets and the saints is the worst of opinions, because these claimants have likened them in this to the tyrants of this world, whose eyes were covered by the darkness of ignorance before meeting death. It does not come to mind that a tyrant who met death and had the veil lifted from him regarding the command of his Lord in this matter would be content that people exalt him with what Allah did not legislate. How then could it be for the Prophets and the truthful ones?

The word "jah" (standing, rank) that people attach to the prophets and the saints when seeking intercession (tawassul), its customary meaning is authority. Or, if you wish, you may say it is the effectiveness of a word with those over whom one has power or with whom one has standing. So it is said, "So-and-so usurped so-and-so's property through his jah," and "So-and-so freed so-and-so from the punishment for his sin through his jah, with the emir or the vizier, for example." Therefore, if someone claims that a person has jah with Allah in this sense, that is a manifest shirk (associating partners with Allah), not a hidden one. Hardly does the linguistic meaning of the word, which is rank and status, come to the mind of any of those who seek intercession. Moreover, there is no sense in seeking intercession through rank and status themselves, because they are not things that benefit. Such a phrase would have meaning only if it were interpreted as one of the attributes of Allah, such as election (ijtiba') and choosing (istifa'), but these have no connection to supplication, and a supplicant cannot intend them in his prayer. Although al-Alusi (al-Alusi) based the permissibility of seeking intercession through the jah of the Prophet ﷺ specifically on that interpretation, what led him to this was only his fear of the tongues of the common people and the abuse of the ignorant, which has no value in the eyes of the knowledgeable. Thus, seeking intercession with the word jah is a bid'ah (innovation) that arose after the three generations, and it carries the suspicion of shirk, may Allah protect us, and the suspicion of deviating from what the Messenger ﷺ brought. Why, then, the insistence on embellishing this innovation?

Some people say: "We have a proof for this that is no more conclusive than it." It is what al-Tirmidhi narrated with his chain to Uthman ibn Hunayf, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "A blind man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Pray to Allah that He cure me.' He said: 'If you wish, I will pray, and if you wish, you may be patient, and that is better for you.' He said: 'Then pray.' So he commanded him to perform ablution well, and to supplicate with this supplication: 'O Allah, I ask You and turn to You through Your Prophet Muhammad, the Prophet of mercy. O Muhammad! I have turned through you to my Lord regarding this need of mine, that it be fulfilled for me. O Allah, so accept his intercession for me.'" Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hadith that is hasan sahih gharib."

We say first: the hadith has been described as gharib (a report transmitted through a single chain). Moreover, it suffices to require caution in acting upon it that the people of the three generations did not do the like of it, and they knew better than us what must be acted upon in this matter. There is no reason for their abstaining from acting upon it except their knowledge that this belongs to the category of asking a living person to join in supplication, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said in the hadith of seeking rain (istisqa'): "We used to seek intercession (tawassul) to You through our Prophet ﷺ and You gave us rain, and now we seek intercession to You through the uncle of Your Prophet, al-Abbas, so give us rain." He said this, may Allah be pleased with him, while al-Abbas was beside him supplicating to Allah, the Exalted. If tawassul were what these claimants claim, 'Umar would have prayed for rain and sought intercession through the Prophet ﷺ, and would not have said, "We used to seek rain through your Prophet." Asking a person to join in supplication is legislated, even from a brother to his brother, and indeed it may be from the higher to the lower, as has been reported in the hadith. There is nothing in it to fear, for the supplicant and the one who joins him in supplication while he is alive are both servants asking Allah, the Exalted, and the partner in supplication is a partner in servitude, not a vizier who manipulates the will of the emir, as they imagine: "Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe" [Al-Saffat: 180].

Then, the matter falls under the category of creed, not under the category of actions. The question in it returns to this: Is it permissible for us to believe that someone other than Allah may be an intermediary between us and Allah in the fulfillment of our needs, or is it not permissible? As for the Book, it is explicit that this belief is one of the beliefs of the polytheists, and it has disparaged it in His saying: "And they worship besides Allah what neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, 'These are our intercessors with Allah'" [Yunus: 18]. And in the surah we recite every day in prayer: "And You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help" [Al-Fatihah: 5]. So there is no seeking of help except from Him. The Book has also stated explicitly that no one possesses for people any benefit or harm from Allah, and this is the tawhid (monotheism) that was the foundation of the chosen Message, as we have explained.

Then, rational proof guides us that Allah, the Exalted, in His actions is not to be compared to rulers and their likes, who change their will because of what those with standing among them obtain. He is exalted above that, may His majesty be great. If an innovator wished to call to this belief, he must establish for it a proof that leads to certainty, either by rational premises that are demonstrative or by transmitted evidence that is mutawatir (widely transmitted). He cannot take a hadith of solitary transmission (ahad) as evidence for a creed, however strong its chain may be, for it is well known among all the imams that solitary reports yield only conjecture: "And conjecture does not avail against the truth in the least" [An-Najm: 28]. The end of his words, may Allah have mercy on him.

Then I reviewed "Iqtida' al-Sirat al-Mustaqim" (The Straight Path) of the eminent imam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah be pleased with him. I found that he mentioned something similar to that, and his expression is: "The means (wasilah) that Allah commanded seeking encompasses means in His worship and in asking Him. So seeking nearness to Him through the righteous deeds He commanded, and through the supplication and intercession of the prophets and the righteous, is not of the category of swearing by His creatures upon Him. Among this category is the people seeking the intercession of the Prophet ﷺ on the Day of Resurrection, for they ask him to intercede for them with Allah, just as in the world they used to ask him to supplicate for them in seeking rain and other matters. The saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: 'We, when we were afflicted with drought, sought intercession to You through our Prophet, and You gave us rain, and now we seek intercession to You through the uncle of our Prophet,' means: we seek intercession through his supplication, his intercession, and his request. We seek intercession to You through the supplication, request, and intercession of his uncle. It does not mean: 'We swear by him,' or anything that goes in this direction, of what is done after his death and in his absence, as some people say: 'I ask You through the jah of so-and-so with You,' and they say: 'We seek intercession to Allah through His prophets and His saints,' and they narrate a fabricated hadith: 'When you ask Allah, ask Him through my jah, for my jah with Allah is vast.' For if this were the tawassul that the Companions used to do, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned, they would have done it after his death, and they would not have turned away from it to al-Abbas, while knowing that asking by him and swearing by him is greater than al-Abbas. So it is known that the tawassul they mentioned is what is done with the living and not the dead, and it is seeking through their supplication and intercession, for the living is asked for that, while the dead is not asked for anything, neither supplication nor anything else. And likewise the hadith of the blind man: he asked the Prophet ﷺ to supplicate for him so that Allah would restore his sight. The Prophet ﷺ taught him a supplication in which he commanded him to ask Allah to accept his prophet's intercession for him. This indicates that the Prophet ﷺ interceded for him, and commanded him to ask Allah to accept his intercession. And his saying, 'I ask You and turn to You through Your Prophet Muhammad, the Prophet of mercy,' means: through his supplication and his intercession, as 'Umar said: 'We used to seek intercession to You through our Prophet.' So the words 'turning' (tawajjuh) and 'seeking intercession' (tawassul) in the two hadiths have one meaning. Then he said: 'O Muhammad! O Messenger of Allah! I turn through you to my Lord regarding my need, that He may fulfill it. O Allah, so accept his intercession for me.' So he asked Allah to accept the intercession of His Prophet for him. As for his saying: 'O Muhammad! O Prophet of Allah!' this and its like is a call (nida'), by which one seeks to summon the one called upon into the heart, (p-4922) so he addresses in the heart the one who is witnessed, as the worshipper says: 'Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings.' A person does this often, addressing whoever he imagines in his mind, even if there is no one outside to hear the address. So the expression of seeking intercession through a person, turning through him, and asking through him, contains generality and ambiguity, and it is an error whose cause is one who did not understand the intent of the Companions. It may mean clinging to him (originally, causing a means through him), because he is a supplicant and intercessor, for example, or because the supplicant is beloved to him, obedient to his command, and follows his example. So the causation is either through the asker's love for him and his following of him, or through the supplication and intercession of the means. And it may mean swearing by him and seeking intercession through his very person, so that the tawassul is not through any action of his nor any action of the asker, but through his person or merely by swearing by him upon Allah. This last is what they disliked and forbade." The end of his words.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[70] ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾: that is, in everything you do and everything you leave undone, especially in committing what He dislikes, let alone what harms His Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿And speak﴾: that is, in every matter of affairs, ﴿words of appropriate justice﴾: that is, upright, true, correct. Al-Qashani said: Sadad in speech, which is truthfulness and correctness, is the source of every happiness and the root of every perfection, for it arises from the purity of the heart, and purity calls for all perfections. Although it falls within the taqwa (God-consciousness) that is commanded, since it is abstention from the vice of lying, and is included under the purification that was expressed by taqwa, it was singled out for mention because of its excellence, as if it were a genus in its own right, just as Gabriel and Michael were singled out from among the angels.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[71] ﴿He will amend for you your deeds and forgive you your sins. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly attained a great attainment.﴾

(p-4923) ﴿He will amend for you your deeds﴾ means: by granting you soundness, perfection and virtues, for no deed is sound at all without truthfulness. Through it every deed becomes sound. ﴿And He will forgive you your sins﴾ means: and He will make them expiated through your uprightness in word and deed, for good deeds remove evil deeds. ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ means: in the commands and prohibitions, among which are these legislations. ﴿Has certainly attained a great attainment﴾ means: in both abodes. Al-Qashani said: that is, he has attained adornment and the attribute of the divine qualities, and that is the great attainment.

Note:

Al-Zamakhshari said: The intent is their prohibition from what they were engaged in regarding the matter of Zaynab, [namely] speaking without purpose and without uprightness of speech, and the urging that their speech be correct in every matter, because guarding the tongue and making speech correct is the head of all good. This verse confirms the one before it. That one was built upon the prohibition of what harms the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this one upon the command to be mindful of Allah, Exalted is He, in guarding the tongue, so that the prohibition and the command follow one another upon them, with the prohibition followed by what contains a warning from the story of Musa (peace be upon him), and the command followed by an eloquent promise, so that the deterrent from harm and the motive to abandon it grow stronger. End of quote.

It is also open to you to add to the intent of the verse what he mentioned another intent, namely their prohibition also from what the hypocrites engaged in of obstruction, discouragement and spreading of rumours during the Battle of the Confederates (ghazwat al-Ahzab), mentioned earlier at the beginning of the surah. In sum, the context includes both of these and others, but what is considered first is that for which the revelation was sent down, and that is what has been mentioned.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 33, verse 72:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[72] ﴿Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it and were apprehensive of it, and man bore it. Indeed, he was ever unjust and ignorant.﴾

﴿Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it and were apprehensive of it, and man bore it. Indeed, he was ever unjust and ignorant.﴾ Abu al-Su'ud said: When He made clear the great importance of obeying Allah and His Messenger, by explaining the fate of those who depart from it, which is a painful punishment, and the example of those who observe it, which is a great triumph, He followed that with an explanation of the great importance of what makes it obligatory, namely the legal obligations, and the difficulty of their matter, by way of illustration. This also indicates that what proceeded from them of obedience and its abandonment proceeded from them after acceptance and commitment. He expressed it as (the trust), to draw attention to the fact that these are rights to be observed, which Allah Most High deposited with the accountable, entrusted them with, and made obligatory upon them, to be received with good obedience and submission. He commanded them to observe and guard them and to discharge them without neglecting any of their rights. He expressed their consideration, in relation to the readiness of the aforementioned heavens and others, by offering it to them, to show extra care for its matter and the desire for their acceptance of it. And [He expressed] their lack of readiness to accept it by refusal and apprehension of it, to magnify its matter and to nurture its grandeur. And [He expressed] their acceptance of it by bearing it, to realize the meaning of the difficulty that is considered in it, by making it of the kind of heavy bodies which employ bodily strength, the greatest and mightiest of which is what is in them of power and might.

The meaning: that this trust is of such great importance that, if it were imposed upon those great bodies, which are an example of strength and might, to observe it, and they were possessed of feeling and perception, they would have refused to accept it and been apprehensive of it. But the speech has been diverted from its usual course, by depicting the hypothetical as though it were realized, in order to increase the realization of the intended meaning through the illustration and its clarification.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and man bore it﴾, i.e. upon its being offered to him, either by considering it in relation to his readiness, or by His imposing it upon him on the Day of the Covenant, i.e. his undertaking and commitment to it despite the weakness of his constitution and the feebleness of his strength. This is either an expression of his acceptance of it in accordance with his innate readiness, or of his acknowledgment by his saying: (Yes). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he was ever unjust and ignorant﴾ is a parenthetical statement between the bearing and its end, to indicate from the outset that he would not fulfil what he pledged and undertook. I.e., he was excessive in injustice and extreme in ignorance; that is, according to the majority of individuals who did not act in accordance with their pure nature or their prior acknowledgment, but not those others who did not alter the nature of Allah. To the first group the Mighty and Majestic One alluded with His saying:

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 33, verse 73 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-4925) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:
[73] ﴿That Allah may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and polytheist women, and that Allah may turn in forgiveness to the believing men and believing women. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿That Allah may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and polytheist women﴾: that is, man bore it so that Allah might punish some of its bearers who did not observe it and did not meet it with obedience. The lam here is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah, the particle indicating an outcome rather than an intended purpose). Although punishment was not the purpose of bearing the trust, once it followed for some of its bearers, it was presented in the form of a purpose, just as purposes follow from the actions they motivate. The meaning is: the outcome of man's bearing the trust was that Allah, exalted is He, would punish these members of his kind because they betrayed the trust and utterly departed from obedience. The second group is alluded to in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that Allah may turn in forgiveness to the believing men and believing women﴾: that is, the outcome of his bearing it was that Allah, exalted is He, would turn to these members of his kind in acceptance, that is, He would accept their repentance, because they had not cast off the yoke of obedience from their necks entirely, and because they made amends for the lapses that proceeded from them, lapses from which a human being rarely remains free by virtue of his nature, and because they remedied them through repentance and returning (to Allah). The name of Majesty is mentioned first to magnify the gravity of the matter and to instill awe; the explicit noun is used in place of a pronoun, second, to highlight the greater concern for the matter of the believers, giving each of the two situations, threat and promise, its due. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾: that is, exceedingly so in forgiveness and mercy, since He turned to them, forgave their lapses, and rewarded their obedience with success. End, summarized, from what Abu al-Su'ud wrote. I have chosen to quote it verbatim because of the excellence of its wording and its mastery of the context, and this is our practice with any refined work: we quote it and do not alter it.

Remaining in the verse are some subtle points which we indicate:

The first: Some of the early generations (al-salaf) interpreted the trust as obedience, others as the obligations, the limits and the religion, and others as knowledge of Him, exalted is He. Ibn Kathir said: All these statements are not contradictory; rather, they are harmonious and all return to the fact that it is the moral obligation (al-taklif) and the acceptance of commands and prohibitions on their conditions, namely that whoever performs them is rewarded and whoever abandons them is punished. End.

It has also been said: the intended meaning of the trust is obedience that encompasses both the natural and the voluntary, because it is inherent in existence, just as the trust is inherent in discharge. By offering it (ʿardh): its solicitation, which encompasses requesting an action from one who has choice and willing its occurrence from another. By bearing it, and betraying it, and refraining from discharging it: so refusing (ibā') is abstention from betrayal and doing what is intended. The meaning is that these bodies, despite their magnitude and strength, refused betrayal and submitted to His command with the submission of such things, since they did not resist His will and His desire in bringing them into being, forming them, and arranging them in various states and diverse shapes, as He said: ﴿They said: We come willingly, obedient﴾ (Fussilat 41:11). Man betrayed it, since he, being a rational animal fit to adapt, did not do what We commanded him; ﴿indeed he was a wrongdoer, ignorant﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:72). The intention of betrayal from bearing it is through likening the trust, before its discharge, to a burden one carries, as one says: "debts have mounted upon him" (rakibathu al-duyun). Al-Zamakhshari established this by saying: As for bearing the trust, it derives from your saying: "So-and-so bears the trust and is charged with it," meaning that he will not return it to its owner until it leaves his responsibility and he is discharged from its obligation. This is because the trust is as if it were riding upon the believers and he is its bearer. Do you not see them saying, "debts have ridden him" and "I have a right upon him"? When he discharges it, it no longer rides him and he no longer bears it. From this also comes their saying: "Hate the right of your brother," because if he loves him, he does not bring it out to him nor render it; but if he hates him, he brings it out and renders it. So the meaning of His saying: ﴿And they refused to bear it﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:72), ﴿and man bore it﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:72): they refused except to discharge it, while man refused except to be a bearer of it who does not discharge it. Then He described him with wrongdoing because he abandoned the discharge of the trust, and with ignorance because he missed what would make him happy while he was able to do it, namely discharging it. End, summarized.

The second: Ibn Kathir related reports from some of the Successors (al-tabi'un) that the offering of the trust to these bodies was real, and that it was said to them: If you do well you will be rewarded, and if you do evil you will be punished. They said: "O Lord! We are not able for this matter; we have no strength, but we are obedient to You." The commentators said: It is not far-fetched that Allah creates in them an understanding of His address, and that this was by way of choice for them; that is why He expressed it as an offering, not as a obligation, so that their disobedience would not follow. End.

(p-4927) Imam Ibn Hazm said in al-Fasl, refuting those who attribute discernment to inanimate things, something of this sort: As for His offering the trust to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and each of them refusing it, we do not know, neither we nor any of mankind, how that was. This is the text of His saying: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves﴾ (al-Kahf 18:51). Whoever burdens himself or burdens others with knowing how creation began, and that it has a beginning resembling nothing at all, and wants to know how it was, has entered into His saying: ﴿and you say with your mouths what you have no knowledge of, and you think it a small matter while it is, with Allah, great﴾ (al-Nur 24:15).

However, we are certain that He, exalted is He, did not offer the trust to the heavens, the earth and the mountains except that He had placed in them discernment for what was offered to them, and a power by which they understand the trust in what was offered to them. When they refused it and feared it, He stripped them of that discernment and that power, and removed from them the obligation of the trust.

He said: This is what His words, mighty and majestic is He, require, and we have nothing more to add to that. End.

A group went further, holding that this is a figure of speech (majaz, figurative usage), as Ibn Abi al-Hadid explained in his commentary on Nahj al-Balagha, and al-Zamakhshari preceded him when he said: Similar to this kind of speech there are many in the language of the Arabs, and the Qur'an came only in their methods and styles. Among that is their saying: "If it were said to fat, 'Where are you going?' it would say, 'I will straighten the crookedness.'" How many proverbs they have on the tongues of animals and inanimate things! Imagining fat conversing is impossible, but the point is that fatness in an animal is something whose ugliness becomes beautiful, just as leanness is something whose beauty becomes ugly. So it depicts the effect of fatness upon it in a manner that is more striking to the hearer's soul, more pleasing to him, more appealing to him, and closer to reality. Likewise the depiction of the greatness of the trust, the difficulty of its matter, the weight of its burden, and the fulfilment of it. End.

The third: al-Razi said: If someone asks: Why did He place the punishment before the repentance at the end of the verse? We say: Since the moral obligation was called a trust, and it is a necessary ruling of the trust that the betrayer is liable, whereas it is not a necessary ruling of the trust that the faithful one who exerts his utmost effort earns a wage, the punishment for betrayal was like the necessary consequence, while the reward for guarding is a kindness, and justice precedes kindness.

The fourth: Several hadiths were narrated concerning the magnification of the trust:

Among them, from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Render the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you." Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi. And from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Four things, if they are in you, then nothing of worldly life that escapes you matters: guarding a trust, truthfulness of speech, good character, and chastity in what you eat." Narrated by Imam Ahmad and al-Tabarani. And from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, to one who asked about the Hour: "When the trust is wasted, then await the Hour." He said: How will it be wasted, O Messenger of Allah? He said: "When the matter is entrusted to other than its people, then await the Hour."

The fifth: Ibn Kathir said: Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak related in the book al-Zuhd that Umar ibn al-Khattab used to forbid swearing by the trust with the utmost prohibition. There is also a hadith traced to Buraydah in this regard: "Whoever swears by the trust is not of us," narrated by Abu Dawud alone. That is, because an oath is not made except by one of His names or one of His attributes; as for other than that, it is disliked or forbidden, as established in its proper place. And Allah knows best.

The sixth: I had previously written something about the verse, in mid-Rabi' al-Awwal of the year 1324 (AH), in a village where a gathering of people of knowledge had assembled. Some people asked about the interpretation of the verse, and there was no tafsir (commentary) available at that time, so I sought help from Allah, exalted is He, read the surah from beginning to end several times, and then wrote what you see.

I wished to include it here to strengthen the discussion, and its text is: In concluding the surah with this verse there is an embellishment of what the scholars of rhetoric call radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr (returning the end to the beginning, a rhetorical device). That is because the opening of this surah was in censuring the hypocrites, and recounting their disgraceful acts (p-4929) and their evil intentions against the Messenger and his companions in the Battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), which is the Battle of the Trench. The Truth, exalted is He, made clear the effect of what was mentioned of the command to piety and of not obeying the hypocrites, and of what they were engaged in, such as the matter of adoption and the like: that they had given covenants and pledges that if they fought they would not flee. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they had already covenanted with Allah before, that they would not turn their backs; and the covenant of Allah is ever to be questioned﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:15). ﴿Say: Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing, and then you will not be given enjoyment except for a little﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:16). When they betrayed their trusts by fleeing, by hindering their brothers, by discouraging them, and by their shameful acts in that battle, Allah, exalted is He, explained at the close of the surah the matter of the trust and the greatness of its importance, and that it has a great station with Allah. That is because whoever gives his own pledge, having covenanted with Allah upon it, souls are reassured by him, trust him, rely upon him, and count him among those who strengthen their backs. Then he turns out to be treacherous, a traitor, a liar, a trifler, who takes the covenants of Allah as mockery and play, forsakes whoever trusted him, colludes with the enemy against him, discourages whoever might be expected to give some assistance, and spreads rumours to weaken resolve and enfeeble determination, so that gossip multiplies and the common people are thrown into confusion. How evil is what he brings, how monstrous is what he commits, and how great is his crime!

It is clear that the greatness of a crime is in proportion to the greatness of its effects, and some of its effects have been mentioned. So in what rank is betrayal? Undoubtedly it is in the lowest of the base abysses. Just as its perpetrator is in the lowest level of the Fire. The trust mentioned in the verse, judging by its context and its preceding passage, is the trust which the hypocrites betrayed in bearing it, and by which they broke their covenant in this event, and whose evil effects in Medina and its people were what they were. Although its wording encompasses what was mentioned and other things, the "man" here refers to the class of the hypocrite whose story has been told in what has been told, and the aim is to blame him for having borne what he bore, then breaking it intentionally and deliberately, wronging himself and being ignorant of the consequence, of the blame that follows it, of the punishment he will meet, and of the fact that this matter is a divine command and a sacred resolve, not a matter for jest.

The meaning of presenting the Trust (al-amanah) to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains is the manifestation of its gravity to these created beings, the enormity of betraying it, and the fear of each of them of the danger of bearing it. They would refuse it, if they were of those who have intellect, even though they are stronger in body, firmer in endurance, and more patient under the afflictions of events, fearing that they might transgress regarding its command or disobey concerning its matter. Man, despite his weakness compared to them, bore it, did not guard it or take care of it, and, despite his weakness, dared to take on what they feared, which was stronger than him. How unjust he is, and how ignorant! The purpose is to accuse him of injustice and ignorance, and of his audacity toward betrayal and his indifference to what the heavens, the earth, and the mountains dread. "Glory be to God, how rebellious he is!" The mention of these great bodies is an exaggeration of the gravity of the Trust, and that if they had intellect, there would have come from them what came. A parallel to this verse in mentioning these three is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ [Maryam: 88] ﴿You have certainly produced [something] monstrous.﴾ [Maryam: 89] ﴿The heavens are about to burst apart from it, the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ [Maryam: 90] ﴿that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son.﴾ [Maryam: 91]

Truly, the casting of the aforementioned meaning in the mold of this wondrous arrangement is one of the miracles of the Revelation and one of its marvels in the domain of eloquence. Its method of pouring meanings into the most delicate words and the most majestic constructions is a style in which it stands alone above every other speech. By this it becomes known that whoever investigates the manner of the presentation to them, whether it was with the placing of intellect within them or not, and the determination of its time, and the manner of their refusal and fear, and the meaning of the reproach of man and charging him with injustice and ignorance after the Trust was presented to him, and that its apparent sense is an option, and so on, all of that is verbal philosophizing, generated by lovers of apparent meanings and words, who are obsessed with exaggerating over their individual terms. Their spending of time on these matters made that the ultimate of their aim and the extent of their knowledge. Thus the meaning was lost to them and they were not guided to it, and they will never find a path to it so long as this is their path. And God speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.
